title: Synthetic workload scaling and observable anchors
body:
Purpose and scope
This note documents a practical methodology for generating repeatable throughput curves for our serving runtime using synthetic workloads. The emphasis here is on stable signal extraction (observable anchors), controlled scaling of concurrency and arrival shape (microbursts -> steady), and a small set of heuristics to minimize non-deterministic noise during comparisons.

Key concepts (short)
- Observable anchors: short, instrumented transactions inserted periodically to anchor end-to-end telemetry (p99 latency, cpu/gpu occupancy, kv-hit ratio).
- Concurrency slices: partitioning a target concurrency into repeated identical cohorts to reduce random scheduling variance.
- Priming window: deterministic prefix sequence used to warm kv-caches and context-alloc paths before measurement windows begin.
- Shape tapering: fading burstiness into plateaued Poisson arrivals to test both transient and steady behavior.

Recommended experiment template
1) Baseline capture (no-load anchors): 2x baseline priming runs with empty traffic to capture infra noise and background activity. 5 minutes each.
2) Priming phase: run deterministic prefix requests for 3–6 minutes depending on model size. Prefixes should be the same set across runs and use fixed RNG seed. Collect KV cache warmup metrics.
3) Ramp: linear ramp to target concurrency over 60s. Use concurrency slices (e.g., for target 64, use 4 slices of 16 with identical request sequences replayed in staggered starts) to avoid single-shot surge effects.
4) Plateau: hold target concurrency for a stable measurement window (recommend 5–10 minutes).
5) Drain: taper down over 30s, then wait 90s idle to let system clear transient resources.
6) Anchor probes: during plateau, every 60s inject 1–2 observable anchors (instrumented short requests) to correlate telemetry across runs.

Load generator config (example fields, phrasing)
- request_set: curated_set_v2 (balanced seq lengths: 32/128/512 tokens at 60/30/10%)
- seed: 442113 (fixed per experiment)
- concurrency_mode: slice
- slices: 4
- slice_size: computed target_concurrency / slices
- arrival_distribution: poisson (lambda computed from concurrency and mean latency)
- ramp_seconds: 60
- plateau_seconds: 600
- anchor_interval_seconds: 60
- anchor_payload: short-echo-16 (deterministic small prompt)
- kv_warmup_prefix_count: 128

Repeatability prescriptions
- Always use a fixed RNG seed and commit the seed in the run metadata.
- Run N >= 5 plateau iterations and compute median + 95% bootstrap CI on mean throughput and p50/p95/p99 latency.
- Keep machine placement fixed where possible (same GPU model, same region, same node-labels). If autoscaling is enabled for the test, record the exact GPU pool and instance ids used.
- Record system-level counters (cpu/gpu utilization, nvlink/pcie saturation metrics, memory pressure) aligned to anchor timestamps.

Warmup heuristics (why and how long)
- Small models: 60–180s of priming may suffice. Large (>20B) models: 3–6 minutes recommended for KV population.
- Use deterministic prefixes sized to touch typical attention window distributions. Example: 60% short prefixes, 30% mid, 10% long.
- Measure cache hit ratio over time; stop warmup when hit ratio slope < 0.5% per minute for two samples.

Handling noise and outliers
- Discard runs with external interference: detected autoscaler activity, network maintenance events, or >10% system interrupts. Flag and rerun.
- Use anchor probes to detect drift: if an anchor’s p99 deviates >20% relative to the historical median, tag run as suspect.
- Analyze tail latencies using trimmed means and median absolute deviation (MAD) to detect cross-run contamination.

Observability anchors (design)
- Anchors should be syntactically small, quick-to-serve prompts that exercise the same kernels as production requests (e.g., attention, kv-lookup). Keep them deterministic to enable tightly aligned telemetry.
- Anchor payloads must be logged separately and indexed by timestamp and run-id. For each anchor record: model_version, route, backend_node, gpu_temp, gpu_power, kv_hit_rate, kernel-time breakdown (where available).

Data capture checklist (what to persist per run)
- run_id, seed, request_set, slices, slice_size, arrival_shape, ramp_seconds, plateau_seconds
- node inventory (gpu model, driver, cudnn/cublas versions)
- full system counters sampled at 1s (cpu/gpu utilization, nvlink/pcie, memory, disk io)
- network counters (latency and packet loss per route)
- model metadata (version, quantization flags, kernel selection hints)
- anchor timeline and outputs

Post-processing and comparison guidance
- Aggregate only plateau window data for final throughput and latency metrics; exclude ramp/drain.
- Compute comparative metrics normalized to tokens/sec and effective concurrency (taking into account queueing delays).
- When comparing two builds, run them interleaved: A1, B1, A2, B2, … to reduce temporal drift effects. Use the same seed and request_set ordering.

Quick troubleshooting log (common failure modes)
- sudden drop in throughput with high p99: check NVLink saturation and kernel fallback logs (non-optimal kernels often cause this).
- throughput oscillation across slices: check slice alignment, potential locking contention in allocator; try increasing slice count to smooth bursts.
- inconsistent latency tails across runs: look for background cron jobs or nightly backups in monitoring; re-run in reserved capacity if possible.

Appendix: small diagnostics commands (examples)
- capture anchors: annotate each anchor with run-id and timestamp; correlate with node /proc/interrupts and dmesg for anomalies.
- quick sanity: run single-slice 1-concurrency with seed fixed and assert p50 ~ local-lab baseline +/- 5% before scaling test.

Open questions / follow-ups
- Formalize anchor payload library: need a minimal set that exercises all hot kernels across model families.
- Integrate anchor-based CI gating for PRs that change kernel selection heuristics.
- Define exact statistical thresholds for automated run rejection (today manually judged).

If this approach looks sensible, next steps: refine anchor payloads, add automatic run tagging for suspected contamination, and create a small runner that enforces the slices + anchor injection semantics.

Notes to reviewers
- This is intentionally prescriptive and pragmatic; aim is to reduce variance for cross-build comparisons rather than to emulate every production path. Feedback on anchor design and slice heuristics especially welcome.
